title: Banks want to ban AI agents, but that takes more than an email
summary: Banks are telling customers to keep AI agents out of their accounts. Without detection, that’s an honor code. Here’s how to detect first, then decide.
body_markdown:
I got an interesting email from my bank this week outlining their new approach to limiting what outside AI agents can do with customer accounts.


The policy itself was pretty clear. Actions initiated by external AI agents “will not be supported on our banking platforms, even if they act on your behalf with your permission.”


Would a bank representative be able to tell if an AI agent logged in or called on a customer’s behalf? Not without designated tools.


Instead, the email ends with a list of recommendations:


- Don’t share your password with AI tools.
- Monitor your accounts.
- Turn on alerts.
- Use MFA.
- Call if something looks off.


That’s the enforcement plan. It’s less a security control and more generic suggestions. Some may even call it an honor code.


To be fair, this bank isn’t alone, joining a growing list of enterprise companies fighting against AI agents. They're not wrong to be concerned. But “we don’t support AI agents” and “we can tell when an AI agent shows up” are two very different sentences. Right now, most financial institutions can only say the first one—and they’re scrambling to figure out how to do the second.


## A ban you can’t see is a ban you can’t enforce


AI agents don’t announce themselves. They say, “I need to dispute a charge on my account,” in a voice that sounds exactly like a real person.


Your IVR can’t tell the difference. Your voiceprint check may not either, especially if the voice was cloned from the real customer. And your human agents? Research puts people’s accuracy at spotting AI-generated media, audio included,[at about 51%](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.16760) . That’s barely better than a coin flip, and generators are getting better every day.


A policy is only as good as your ability to enforce it.


## Real customers are already sending agents


This isn’t a future problem, and you can’t cross your fingers and hope customers stop using agents they’re already adopting. 74% of consumers say they’d hand routine tasks to an AI agent, according to[Accenture](https://www.accenture.com/en/insights/consulting/talk-my-ai-agent) .[Salesforce](https://www.salesforce.com/service/resources/state-of-service-ai-agents-edition/) reports 66% of service organizations already use agentic AI on their own side of the call.[Gartner](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2025-03-05-gartner-predicts-agentic-ai-will-autonomously-resolve-80-percent-of-common-customer-service-issues-without-human-intervention-by-20290) expects 80% of common service issues to be handled without a person by 2029.


We see it in production, too. A global bank using Reality Defender identified 185% more synthetic voice callers in September 2026 than in September 2025, and that number is expected to climb. A customer email isn’t going to change that.


## Why blanket blocking backfires


You could block every AI caller, but should you? Consider this:


**You cut off real customers.** Someone who sent an agent to update their direct deposit details still needs it done. Hang up on the agent and the request comes right back, through a more expensive channel, with a more frustrated customer.


**You don’t stop the bad guys.** Fraudsters don’t care about account security policies, and an impersonator with a cloned voice sounds exactly like the customer you’re trying to protect. A “no AI” rule does nothing about that without detection.


**You still pay for it.** Legit or not, AI calls cost money, whether they tie up a live agent or your own automation. AI agents are also persistent. They don’t get tired, don’t give up, and will keep calling back until they get what they came for. And when one lands on your own AI agent, the two can go back and forth, burning through tokens. That’s the upside of seeing these calls. An unenforced ban doesn’t make the cost go away. It just makes it harder to track.


## Detect first, then decide


You can’t set a sensible policy for traffic you can’t see, so start with the signal. Reality Defender’s[RealCall](https://www.realitydefender.com/product/realcall) analyzes live call audio inside your existing telephony or contact center stack and tells you whether the voice on the line is human or AI-generated in real time. That signal goes back to your platform so you can route, flag, or step up verification before the call reaches a person.


So what do you actually do once you know? That part is up to you, but here’s how contact centers are putting the signal to work:


**Block what doesn’t belong.** Not every AI caller, just the ones your policy rules out. A synthetic voice trying to get past authentication, or an agent attempting a high-risk change like a wire transfer or payout update, gets stopped before it ties up a live agent or touches an account.


**Route it.** Send AI callers to an automated lane so routine requests, like a balance check or a statement request, still get handled without pulling a live agent off the queue.


**Redirect it.** Point AI callers to a web-based flow where the customer confirms the agent is acting on their behalf before anything on the account changes.


**Step it up.** At authentication, use the signal alongside voice biometrics. A cloned voice that matches a voiceprint triggers extra verification instead of getting a free pass.


**Slow it down.** If a synthetic voice reaches a live agent, prompt the agent with one clear action, like pausing a payout change or calling the customer back on the number on file.


Your organization sets the policy. Reality Defender supplies the signal.


## Know who’s on the line first


These financial institutions have the right instincts. AI agents do change the game for financial services, but a policy without detection is just a request. Whether you want to block, allow, or route AI agents, you first need to know they’re there.


Otherwise it’s an honor system, and the bad guys don’t play by the honor system.
